source_text:
Haec et huiusmodi propudia nobis non licet nec audire, etiam pluribus turpe defendere est: ea enim de castis fingitis et pudicis, quae fieri non crederemus, nisi de uobis probaretis.
nam quod religioni nostrae hominem noxium et crucem eius adscribitis, longe de uicinia ueritatis erratis, qui putatis Deum credi aut meruisse noxium aut potuisse terrenum.
ne ille miserabilis, cuius in homine mortali spes omnis innititur; totum enim eius auxilium cum extincto homine finitur.
Aegyptii sane hominem sibi quem colant eligunt: illum unum propitiant, illum de omnibus consulunt, illi uictimas caedunt. at ille, qui ceteris deus, sibi certe homo est, uelit nolit: nec enim conscientiam suam decipit, si fallit alienam.
etiam principibus et regibus, non ut magnis et electis uiris, sicut fas est, sed ut deis turpiter adulatio falsa blanditur, cum et praeclaro uiro honor uerius et optimo amor dulcius praebeatur. sic eorum numen uocant, ad imagines supplicant, genium, id est daemonem eorum implorant, et est eis tutius per Iouis genium peierare quam regis. cruces etiam nec colimus nec optamus.
uos plane, qui ligneos deos consecratis, cruces ligneas ut deorum uestrorum partes forsitan adoratis.
nam et signa ipsa et cantabra et uexilla castrorum quid aliud quam inauratae cruces sunt et ornatae? tropaea uestra uictricia non tantum simplicis crucis faciem, uerum et adfixi hominis imitantur.
signum sane crucis naturaliter uisimus in naui, cum uelis tumentibus uehitur, cum expansis palmulis labitur: et cum erigitur iugum, crucis signum est, et cum homo porrectis manibus Deum pura mente ueneratur. ita signo crucis aut ratio naturalis innititur aut uestra religio formatur.
thought_title: The Cross and the Folly of Deifying Humans
orientation: Octavius is answering Caecilius's charge that Christians worship a crucified criminal, and he now turns the charge of cross-worship back onto pagan practice.
pass_a_gloss: These things and things of this kind, shameful acts, it is not permitted for us even to hear, and even to defend them before many people is shameful: for you invent those things about chaste and modest people, which we would not believe happen, unless you proved them about yourselves. For as to the fact that you attribute to our religion a guilty man and his cross, you wander far from the neighborhood of truth, you who think that God is believed either to have deserved to be guilty or to have been able to be earthly. Truly that man is wretched, whose whole hope rests on a mortal man; for all his help is ended together with the dead man. The Egyptians indeed choose for themselves a man whom they may worship: that one alone they propitiate, that one they consult about all things, to that one they slaughter victims. But he who is a god to the others is certainly a man to himself, whether he wishes or not: for he does not deceive his own conscience, even if he deceives another's. Even to princes and kings, not as to great and chosen men, as is right, but as to gods, shamefully false flattery fawns, although to a distinguished man honor is more truly offered and to the best man love is more sweetly offered. Thus they call their deity, they pray to images, they invoke their genius, that is their demon, and it is safer for them to swear falsely by the genius of Jupiter than by the king. Crosses also we neither worship nor desire. You plainly, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps adore wooden crosses as parts of your gods. For both the standards themselves and the banners and the flags of the camps, what else are they than gilded crosses and decorated ones? Your victorious trophies imitate not only the appearance of a simple cross, but also of an affixed man. The sign of the cross surely we see naturally in a ship, when it is carried along with swelling sails, when it glides with outspread oars: and when a yoke is raised, it is the sign of the cross, and when a man with outstretched hands venerates God with pure mind. Thus on the sign of the cross either natural reason rests or your religion is formed.

choices.why: The word denotes disgraceful, indecent things; 'shameful acts' keeps the moral revulsion without modernizing to a weaker term.

choices.english: you wander far from the neighborhood of truth
choices.why: The spatial metaphor of 'neighborhood' is deliberate and vivid; keeping it literal preserves the rhetorical force.
rejected: you are far from the truth
you stray far from truth's vicinity

choices.why: The compact Latin idiom needs full expansion in English to keep the force of the contrast.

choices.english: their genius, that is their demon
choices.why: The source explicitly equates genius with demon; keeping both terms preserves the theological point that the pagan guardian spirit is a demon.
rejected: their guardian spirit, that is their evil spirit

choices.why: Both are military standards; distinguishing them as 'banners' and 'flags' keeps the enumeration visible without merging them.
Palmula is specifically the blade of an oar; 'oar-blades' is precise and avoids the misleading 'palms'.

pass_b_english: We are not permitted even to hear of such shameful acts as these, and it is disgraceful for many to defend them. You invent stories about people who are chaste and modest that we would never believe happened, unless you proved them true of yourselves.

As for your charge that you ascribe a criminal and his cross to our religion, you wander far from the neighborhood of truth when you think that God could be believed either to have deserved punishment as a criminal or to have been capable of earthly existence.
How pitiable is the man whose whole hope rests on a mortal human being! All his help comes to an end when that human being dies.

The Egyptians, to be sure, choose a man for themselves to worship. They propitiate him alone, consult him above all others, and slaughter victims for him. But he who is a god to everyone else is certainly a man to himself, whether he wishes or not. He does not deceive his own conscience, even if he deceives someone else's.

Even princes and kings are shamefully courted with false flattery—not as great and chosen men, as is proper, but as gods. Yet honor is more truly given to a distinguished man, and love is more sweetly offered to a good one. So people call their deity by name, kneel before their images, and implore their genius, that is, their demon. And they think it safer to swear falsely by the genius of Jupiter than by the king.

We neither worship crosses nor wish for them. You, however, who consecrate wooden gods, perhaps adore wooden crosses as parts of your gods. For what else are your standards, banners, and camp flags but crosses gilded and decorated? Your victorious trophies imitate not only the shape of a simple cross, but also of a man nailed to it.

We certainly see the sign of the cross naturally in a ship when it sails with swelling sails and glides along with outspread oar-blades. And when a yoke is lifted up, it is the sign of the cross; and when a man worships God with pure mind and outstretched hands. Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your own religion is shaped by it.

problems.quote: and for most of us it is a disgrace to defend ourselves against them.
problems.why: Latin says it is disgraceful for many to defend the acts; English flips agency to defending oneself.
problems.fix: and it is disgraceful for many to defend them.

problems.quote: to have been made of earth
problems.why: terrenum means earthly/mortal, not made of earth; it contrasts with divine nature.
problems.fix: to have been capable of earthly existence
problems.ruling: terrēnum = earthly/mortal, not ‘made of earth’; translation changes meaning

problems.quote: our religion worships a criminal and his cross
problems.source_quote: nam quod religioni nostrae hominem noxium et crucem eius adscribitis
problems.why: Latin says you ascribe a harmful man and his cross to our religion; English adds worship, changing agency.
problems.fix: you ascribe a criminal and his cross to our religion
problems.ruling: Latin 'adscribitis' means 'you ascribe/attribute'; English 'worships' changes agency from accusers to believers.

edits.old: and for most of us it is a disgrace to defend ourselves against them.
edits.new: and it is disgraceful for many to defend them.

edits.old: to have been made of earth.
edits.new: to have been capable of earthly existence.

edits.old: our religion worships a criminal and his cross
edits.new: you ascribe a criminal and his cross to our religion

fixed: Agency: 'etiam pluribus turpe defendere est' means it is disgraceful for many to defend the acts, not for us to defend ourselves.
Mistranslation: 'terrenum' means earthly/mortal, not made of earth.
Agency: 'adscribitis' means you ascribe, not our religion worships.

problems.quote: and implore their genius, that is their demon
problems.source_quote: genium, id est daemonem eorum implorant
problems.why: 'daemonem' here refers to the attendant spirit/guardian spirit, not 'demon' in the Christian evil sense; Octavius equates pagan genius with demons but 'daemon' in this period can mean neutral spirit.
problems.fix: and implore their genius, that is, their demon
problems.ruling: Translates daemon as 'demon', altering neutral spirit to evil

problems.quote: So the sign of the cross is grounded either in natural reason or in your own religion
problems.source_quote: ita signo crucis aut ratio naturalis innititur aut uestra religio formatur
problems.why: 'innititur' means 'rests/leans upon', 'formatur' means 'is shaped/formed'; the English reverses the logic—natural reason rests on the cross sign, and their religion is shaped by it.
problems.fix: Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your own religion is shaped by it
problems.ruling: Reverses direction: Latin says reason rests on sign, English says sign grounded in reason

edits.old: and implore their genius, that is their demon.
edits.new: and implore their genius, that is, their demon.

edits.old: So the sign of the cross is grounded either in natural reason or in your own religion.
edits.new: Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your own religion is shaped by it.

fixed: Added comma after 'that is' to clarify the appositive reading of 'daemonem' as the genius/attendant spirit, matching the source's 'genium, id est daemonem eorum implorant'.

Corrected the reversed logic: source 'ita signo crucis aut ratio naturalis innititur aut uestra religio formatur' means natural reason rests on the sign of the cross, and their religion is shaped by it.

last_rejected.quote: As for your charge that you ascribe a criminal and his cross to our religion
last_rejected.source_quote: nam quod religioni nostrae hominem noxium et crucem eius adscribitis
last_rejected.why: English 'your charge that you ascribe' misattributes: source says 'you ascribe to our religion', spoken by Octavius against opponents.
last_rejected.fix: As for your ascribing a criminal and his cross to our religion
last_rejected.ruling: Latin says 'you ascribe ... to our religion'; English adds 'your charge' but meaning of accusation remains

last_rejected.quote: How pitiable is the man whose whole hope rests on a mortal human being!
last_rejected.source_quote: ne ille miserabilis, cuius in homine mortali spes omnis innititur
last_rejected.why: Source is exclamatory 'ne ille miserabilis' = 'wretched is he' (the one who hopes in mortal man), not 'How pitiable is the man'.
last_rejected.fix: Wretched is he whose every hope rests on a mortal human being!
last_rejected.ruling: Latin exclamation 'ne ille miserabilis' = 'wretched/poor thing'; English 'How pitiable' conveys same sense

last_rejected.quote: and when a man worships God with pure mind and outstretched hands
last_rejected.source_quote: et cum homo porrectis manibus Deum pura mente ueneratur
last_rejected.why: English inverts: source is 'with outstretched hands, with pure mind worships God'—'pura mente' modifies worship, not 'with outstretched hands'.
last_rejected.fix: and when a man with outstretched hands worships God with pure mind
last_rejected.ruling: Both 'pura mente' and 'porrectis manibus' modify worship; English lists both, order irrelevant

last_rejected.quote: Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your own religion is shaped by it
last_rejected.source_quote: ita signo crucis aut ratio naturalis innititur aut uestra religio formatur
last_rejected.why: English 'or' suggests exclusive alternatives; Latin 'aut...aut' = 'either...or' but 'innititur' = 'rests upon/leans on', 'formatur' = 'is formed/shaped by'. The sense is that natural reason is supported by the cross-sign, OR pagan religion is shaped by it (accusation). English 'your own religion is shaped by it' loses the force that pagan religion is derivative/imitative.
last_rejected.fix: Thus either natural reason rests upon the sign of the cross, or your religion is modeled on it
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'aut ratio naturalis innititur aut uestra religio formatur' = 'either natural reason rests on the sign, or your religion is formed by it'; English matches
